context.heading: A bride in black
context.body: Joel compares the land to a betulah ("virgin"), a young woman in sackcloth mourning "the husband of her youth." She is probably a betrothed bride whose groom died before the wedding. The grief is for a future that was about to begin and is now gone, which is exactly what a ruined harvest meant for a farming family.

context.heading: When worship itself stops
context.body: The grain and drink offerings were made from flour, oil and wine. With fields stripped and vines bare, the priests had nothing to offer (v. 13). For Israel this was more than an economic disaster; the daily rhythm of fellowship with God at the temple was breaking down.

context.heading: Call a holy fast
context.body: Qadash ("consecrate") means to set something apart for God. Joel tells the priests to set apart a fast and gather everyone, elders and ordinary residents alike, to the temple. National disaster becomes a summons to come before God together, not just to tighten belts.

theology.title: The Lord of creation
theology.body: Joel assumes that locusts, drought and harvest are not outside God's hand. The same God who fed Israel in the wilderness can withhold grain and wine. Scripture also warns against reading every disaster as a specific punishment (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:3), but Joel treats this one as a wake up call.

theology.title: A preview of the Day
theology.body: Joel calls the disaster a foretaste of "the Day of the LORD" (v. 15), the time God steps in to judge and set things right. Later prophets and the New Testament keep that phrase for the final day (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Present troubles are meant to make us ready for that one.

application.title: Tell your children
application.body: Joel's first instruction is to pass the story down for three generations (v. 3). Disasters fade from memory quickly unless someone names what God taught through them.
application.question: What hard season in your family's story have you never told your kids about, including what God did in it?

application.title: Wake up, drunkards
application.body: Joel calls out the people least likely to notice trouble: those numbing themselves while the vines die (v. 5). Comfort habits can keep us from feeling what we ought to feel.
application.question: What do you reach for that keeps you from noticing what God might be saying through a hard situation?

application.title: Grief that goes somewhere
application.body: Joel does not tell people to stop mourning; he tells them to bring their mourning to God's house and cry out (v. 14). Lament aimed at God is not the same as despair.
application.question: Where are you grieving alone that you could bring to God and to your church instead?

context.heading: An army that looks like horses
context.body: Locusts resemble tiny horses, and several languages still call them that (German Heupferd, "hay horse"). Joel describes the swarm as a cavalry army scaling walls and entering windows. Interpreters differ on whether chapter 2 is the same locusts described as an army, a future human invader, or a picture of the final Day. Many see more than one layer.

context.heading: He relents
context.body: Nacham ("relents") is used of God changing course in response to repentance, as with Nineveh (Jonah 3:10). Joel's "Who knows?" (v. 14) is honest: repentance is not a lever that forces God's hand. It is an appeal to His revealed character in Exodus 34:6.

context.heading: Repaying the eaten years
context.body: Shalam ("repay") is related to shalom and means to make whole, to compensate in full. God calls the locusts "My great army" and then promises to restore what they consumed. He does not just stop the damage; He makes up the loss.

theology.title: The Spirit for all kinds of people
theology.body: In the Old Testament the Spirit came on chosen leaders: prophets, judges, kings. Joel promises the Spirit on sons and daughters, young and old, even servants, echoing Moses' wish in Numbers 11:29. Peter announced at Pentecost that this had begun (Acts 2:16–21). Christians differ on whether the cosmic signs of verses 30–31 were fulfilled then or still await the end.

theology.title: Whoever calls will be saved
theology.body: Verse 32 makes rescue as wide as calling on the LORD's name. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:13 and applies "the LORD" to Jesus, a striking claim that Jesus shares the identity of Israel's God. The door Joel opened for Israel is opened to Jew and Gentile alike.

application.title: Torn hearts, not torn shirts
application.body: Tearing clothes was the public sign of grief. God wants the inner change the gesture was meant to show (v. 13).
application.question: What religious habit do you keep up that has quietly replaced real change of heart?

application.title: Everyone in the room
application.body: Joel summons infants, elders, and even a bride and groom on their wedding day (v. 16). No one is too busy or too happy to come before God.
application.question: What important event in your calendar would you find hardest to set aside to seek God?

application.title: The years the locusts ate
application.body: Many people carry regret over wasted or stolen years: addiction, a bad marriage, a lost decade. God's promise to restore does not erase the past, but it means the past is not the final word.
application.question: Which lost years have you written off that you could bring to God for Him to redeem?

context.heading: Plowshares into swords
context.body: Joel reverses the famous image of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3. Before peace comes, the nations are summoned to arm themselves for a final confrontation with God. Farm tools become weapons, and even the weak boast they are warriors. It is ironic: no amount of arming will matter in this battle.

context.heading: The lion's roar
context.body: Sha'ag ("roar") is the sound of a lion over its prey. Amos opens his book with the same line (Amos 1:2), and the two prophets may be deliberately linked. The roar that makes the earth shake is, for God's people, the sound of their refuge (machseh) arriving.

context.heading: Slaves sold to Greece
context.body: Joel charges Phoenician and Philistine traders with selling Judeans to the "Greeks" (Hebrew Javan, Ionia). Greek trade in the eastern Mediterranean goes back centuries, so the reference does not settle Joel's date. It shows how cheaply the nations treated Judah's children, trading a girl for a drink of wine (v. 3).

theology.title: The Judge of all nations
theology.body: God gathers every nation and judges them for what they did to His people and His land. The book of Revelation borrows Joel's harvest and winepress images for the final judgment (Revelation 14:14–20). History is not a random struggle of empires; it has a Judge, and accounts will be settled.

theology.title: A river from God's house
theology.body: Joel ends with water flowing from the temple, turning a dry valley green. Ezekiel 47 and Zechariah 14:8 expand the picture, and Revelation 22:1 shows the river of life flowing from God's throne. The God who sent drought in chapter 1 will one day make His presence the source of life for the whole land.

application.title: Injustice is noticed
application.body: Joel names specific crimes: children sold, treasures stolen, people scattered. God remembers what history books forget.
application.question: Whose suffering have you assumed nobody will ever answer for, and how does God's judgment change how you carry it?

application.title: Refuge in the shaking
application.body: The same voice that shakes heaven and earth is a stronghold for His people (v. 16). Fear and safety can come from the same God, depending on where you stand.
application.question: When world events shake you, what do you actually run to first?

application.title: Never again
application.body: God promises that invaders will never again pass through Jerusalem (v. 17), and that His people will never again be put to shame (2:26–27). The future He describes is permanent, not another cycle of loss.
application.question: How would your worries about the future change if you truly believed the ending is already secure?
